reviewed.source_quote: compresses the third cranial nerve and posterior cerebral artery downward, the ipsilateral pupil becomes progressively dilated and responds sluggishly to light
reviewed.note: Book p. 703 supports ipsilateral pupillary dilation from uncal herniation compressing CN III. The 'petroclinoid ligament' in the marked answer is not mentioned in the chapter (book: tentorial edge, PCA, hippocampal gyrus, p. 694). The contralateral extensor posturing attributed to peduncle compression is not stated either.

reviewed.source_quote: interrupting the cerebral peduncle (particularly the fibers that project to the leg) on the side opposite the original temporal lobe lesion
reviewed.note: Book p. 703: midbrain pushed against the opposite tentorial edge (Kernohan notch), causing hemiparesis ipsilateral to the lesion; p. 703 also says that with ipsilateral dilated pupil and hemiparesis the lesion is on the side of the abnormal pupil.

reviewed.source_quote: affect pupillary function earlier and more noticeably than the extrinsic eye movements subserved by this cranial nerve
reviewed.note: Book p. 694 supports early ipsilateral pupillary involvement with a sluggish then widely dilated pupil (Hutchinson pupil, sparing of sympathetics). The claim that the peripheral/superficial parasympathetic fibers on CN III are the reason is not in the chapter, which lists several possible mechanisms (tentorial edge, PCA, hippocampal gyrus, traction).

reviewed.source_quote: This results in hemiparesis ipsilateral to the original lesion (Kernohan notch phenomenon)
reviewed.note: Book p. 703. The eponym Kernohan-Woltman is not used in the chapter (only Kernohan notch). Near-duplicate of ch23-002.

reviewed.source_quote: decerebrate rigidity results from brainstem transection at the collicular level, below the red nuclei but leaving intact the pontine reticular formation and vestibular nuclei
reviewed.note: Book p. 701 supports decerebrate rigidity (experimental) below the red nuclei with unchecked vestibular nuclei; decorticate rigidity is described as hemisphere plus diencephalon lesion (p. 700). The chapter does not describe rubrospinal-driven upper limb flexion, and warns (p. 700) that these postures are often produced by metabolic disorders and lack the structural implications their names suggest.

Subfalcine herniation, ACA compression and the Cushing response are not mentioned in Chapter 23. Only p. 709 says posterior fossa masses may cause downward tonsillar herniation with infarction of tonsils, medulla and upper cervical cord.

reviewed.source_quote: Irrigation of cold water into the right external auditory canal induces tonic deviation of the eyes to the right in this patient with coma
reviewed.note: Video legend p. 714 (comatose patient: tonic deviation toward the cold ear, no nystagmus; awake patient would show nystagmus). Technique 50 mL ice water, head at 30 degrees on p. 696; absent eye movement during 1 minute of observation as a brain death criterion on p. 711. The COWS mnemonic is not in the chapter.

reviewed.source_quote: elongation and rupture of the paramedian perforating arteries feeding these structures, resulting in infarction and hemorrhages (Duret) in the tegmentum of the midbrain
reviewed.note: Book p. 704 (also p. 703 and Fig. 23-6 legend: stretching of perforating branches of the basilar artery). The 'tethered basilar trunk' wording is an inference not stated in the chapter.

new_questions.vignette: A 59-year-old man is mute and motionless but awake and aware of his surroundings. He answers questions by moving his eyes vertically and blinking. Horizontal eye movements are impaired. An EEG shows a normal waking pattern.
new_questions.question: Which lesion pattern best explains this state?
options: Bilateral lesions of the descending motor pathways in the basis pontis, sparing the dorsal reticular formation
Bilateral lesions of the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation
Bilateral lesions of the anterior cingulate gyri
Bilateral lesions of the dorsomedial medulla

explanation.why_correct: In locked-in syndrome the lesions involve the descending motor pathways bilaterally in the basis pontis but spare the more dorsal reticular formation, so the patient remains awake and aware. Horizontal gaze is impaired by involvement of the paramedian pontine reticular formation, while vertical eye and lid movements remain available for communication.
distractors: Involvement of the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation produces akinetic mutism, in which the patient seems awake but is silent and motionless, without the preserved purposeful vertical eye signaling and awareness of locked-in syndrome.
Anterior cingulate lesions cause akinetic mutism with frontal release signs, not de-efferentation with preserved eye-based responses.
The dorsomedial medulla damage is associated with ataxic breathing and respiratory failure rather than preserved alertness with quadriplegia.
explanation.key_point: Locked-in syndrome: bilateral basis pontis lesion that spares the dorsal reticular formation; alertness and vertical eye movements are preserved.

new_questions.source_quote: These lesions involve the descending motor pathways bilaterally in the basis pontis but spare the more dorsal reticular formation

new_questions.vignette: A 47-year-old woman is mute, quadriparetic and aware. Unlike most locked-in patients, she also has bilateral ptosis and cannot move her eyes vertically or horizontally.
new_questions.question: Which level of the brainstem is most likely affected?

explanation.why_correct: In locked-in syndrome due to mesencephalic lesions, bilateral ptosis and vertical as well as horizontal ophthalmoplegia are present, unlike the pontine form in which vertical eye and lid movements are spared.
distractors: A basis pontis lesion typically spares vertical eye movements and eyelid movements, which patients use to communicate.
Medullary lesions are associated with respiratory failure and loss of automatic breathing, not preserved awareness with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis.
Cerebellar vermis lesions do not cause quadriparesis with bilateral ptosis and ophthalmoplegia.
explanation.key_point: Locked-in syndrome with bilateral ptosis and vertical plus horizontal ophthalmoplegia points to the midbrain.

new_questions.source_quote: In locked-in syndrome due to mesencephalic lesions, bilateral ptosis and vertical (as well as horizontal) ophthalmoplegia are present

new_questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man after a hypoxic injury appears awake but lies silent and motionless. His eyes dart toward the examiner as she approaches, but he does not respond to questions. He has a grasp reflex and a sucking reflex, with little evidence of damage to the descending motor pathways.
new_questions.question: Which pair of regions is most characteristically involved bilaterally in this condition?
options: Anterior cingulate gyri and the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation
Occipital poles and the calcarine cortex
Cerebellar hemispheres and the dentate nuclei

explanation.why_correct: Akinetic mutism results from bilateral lesions of the frontal region (anterior cingulate gyri), the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation, the globus pallidus or the hypothalamus. Frontal release signs such as grasp or sucking reflexes may be present.
distractors: Basis pontis and pyramidal damage produces de-efferentation (locked-in state) with obvious motor pathway damage, which is largely absent in akinetic mutism.
Occipital lesions cause visual loss but not a state of silence and akinesia with frontal release signs.
Cerebellar lesions cause ataxia and do not produce this state of unresponsive wakefulness.
explanation.key_point: Akinetic mutism: silent, motionless, eyes following movement, frontal release signs; bilateral anterior cingulate, diencephalomesencephalic, pallidal or hypothalamic lesions.

new_questions.source_quote: Lesions that cause akinetic mutism bilaterally affect the frontal region (anterior cingulate gyri), the diencephalomesencephalic reticular formation, the globus pallidus, or the hypothalamus

new_questions.vignette: A comatose 70-year-old man with a cerebellar hemorrhage has completely irregular breathing, with inspiratory gasps of different depth and length intermixed with apneic pauses. He is on the verge of respiratory failure.
new_questions.question: Damage to which structure produces this breathing pattern?
options: Lateral tegmentum of the lower pons

explanation.why_correct: Ataxic breathing, completely irregular and often present in agonal patients, heralds complete respiratory failure and follows damage of the dorsomedial medulla. Cerebellar or pontine hemorrhage, trauma and posterior fossa tumors are common causes.
distractors: Lateral tegmental lesions of the lower pons produce apneustic breathing, with a long inspiratory pause.
Bilateral hemispheric dysfunction causes posthyperventilation apnea and Cheyne-Stokes breathing, which is regular and waxing and waning.
Midbrain and pontine lesions are associated with prolonged rapid hyperpnea rather than an irregular ataxic pattern.
explanation.key_point: Ataxic (Biot) breathing indicates dorsomedial medullary damage and impending respiratory failure.

new_questions.source_quote: This respiratory abnormality, often present in agonal patients, heralds complete respiratory failure and follows damage of the dorsomedial medulla

new_questions.vignette: A comatose patient with a basilar artery occlusion breathes with a long pause at full inspiration, holds the air for several seconds, and then releases it.
new_questions.question: Which brainstem lesion is most typically associated with this breathing pattern?
options: Lateral tegmentum of the lower half of the pons

explanation.why_correct: Apneustic breathing, characterized by a long inspiratory pause with retention of air for several seconds before release, appears with lesions of the lateral tegmentum of the lower half of the pons.
distractors: Dorsomedial medullary damage produces ataxic breathing with irregular gasps and apneic periods.
Bilateral thalamic dysfunction is more typical of Cheyne-Stokes respiration with regularly waxing and waning breaths.
High cervical cord lesions are described in the chapter with loss of automatic breathing during sleep (Ondine curse), not with apneustic breathing.
explanation.key_point: Apneustic breathing localizes to the lateral tegmentum of the lower pons.

new_questions.source_quote: Apneustic breathing is characterized by a long inspiratory pause, after which the air is retained for several seconds and then released. This abnormality appears with lesions of the lateral tegmentum of the lower half of the pons

new_questions.vignette: A 66-year-old woman with a large supratentorial mass has periods of hyperpnea alternating regularly with shorter apneic periods. During the hyperpneic phase she becomes more alert and her miotic pupils dilate toward normal.
new_questions.question: Which level of dysfunction is this breathing pattern most likely to reflect?
options: Bilateral hemispheric or bilateral thalamic dysfunction
Lateral tegmentum of the lower pons

explanation.why_correct: Cheyne-Stokes respiration may follow bilateral widespread cortical lesions but is more likely associated with bilateral thalamic dysfunction, and with descending pathway lesions down to the upper pons. In patients with supratentorial masses it may indicate incipient transtentorial herniation.
distractors: Dorsomedial medullary damage produces ataxic breathing, which is irregular rather than regularly waxing and waning.
Apneustic breathing is a sustained inspiratory pause caused by lower pontine tegmental lesions.
Unilateral medullary tegmental infarcts have produced loss of automatic breathing during sleep (Ondine curse), not this pattern.
explanation.key_point: Cheyne-Stokes breathing reflects bilateral forebrain or diencephalic dysfunction and may herald transtentorial herniation.

new_questions.source_quote: This respiratory pattern may follow bilateral widespread cortical lesions but is more likely to be associated with bilateral thalamic dysfunction

new_questions.vignette: A comatose 64-year-old hypertensive man with quadriparesis has pinpoint pupils. When examined with a magnifying glass, the pupils constrict to light. Imaging shows a large hemorrhage.
new_questions.question: Where is the hemorrhage most likely located?

explanation.why_correct: Pinpoint pupils that still constrict to light under magnification may occur with pontine hemorrhage, from a combination of sympathetic damage and parasympathetic irritation. Pontine tegmental lesions cause small pupils by interrupting descending sympathetic pathways.
distractors: Tectal or pretectal lesions abolish the light reflex and produce midsize or slightly large pupils.
Uncal herniation causes an ipsilateral widely dilated pupil with a sluggish or absent light reflex, not pinpoint pupils.
Occipital lesions do not alter the pupillary light reflex, which depends on the midbrain and oculomotor nerve.
explanation.key_point: Pinpoint but light-reactive pupils in coma point to a pontine lesion such as pontine hemorrhage.

new_questions.source_quote: Pinpoint pupils, when observed with a magnifying glass, may be seen to constrict to light, may occur with pontine hemorrhage

new_questions.vignette: A comatose 55-year-old woman has intermittent, brisk, bilateral downward jerks of both eyes with a slow return to midposition. Horizontal eye movements elicited by the doll's eye maneuver are preserved.
new_questions.question: Which localization is this type of eye movement thought to be specific, but not pathognomonic, for?
options: Bilateral cerebral damage with intact brainstem

explanation.why_correct: Ocular bobbing with preserved horizontal eye movements (typical bobbing) is thought to be specific but not pathognomonic of acute pontine injury. Atypical bobbing, with absent horizontal movements, is less helpful for localization.
distractors: Pretectal pseudobobbing with hydrocephalus has a V pattern (down and in), a faster rate and pretectal signs, and is distinguished from true bobbing.
Bilateral cerebral damage with an intact brainstem is associated with periodic alternating gaze (ping-pong gaze), a horizontal oscillation.
Frontal eye fields mediate conjugate deviation and the quick phase of nystagmus, not bobbing.
explanation.key_point: Typical ocular bobbing (preserved horizontal movements) points to acute pontine injury.

new_questions.source_quote: Typical ocular bobbing, which is associated with preserved horizontal eye movements, is thought to be specific but not pathognomonic of acute pontine injury

new_questions.vignette: A comatose 68-year-old man has a right hemiparesis. His eyes are deviated to the left. The doll's eye maneuver brings the eyes past the midline to the right, and caloric testing also overcomes the deviation.
new_questions.question: Where is the lesion most likely located?

explanation.why_correct: With hemispheric lesions the eyes look toward the lesion (away from the hemiparetic side) but can be brought to the other side with the oculocephalic maneuver or caloric testing. Pontine gaze palsy cannot be overcome by either maneuver.
distractors: Lower pontine tegmental lesions cause a horizontal gaze palsy toward the side of the lesion, so the eyes look toward the hemiparetic side, and neither oculocephalic nor caloric testing overcomes it.
A right pontine lesion would also produce a gaze palsy that cannot be overcome, with eyes directed toward the hemiparetic side.
A right hemispheric lesion would drive the eyes to the right, toward the lesion and away from the right-sided hemiparesis.
explanation.key_point: In coma, eyes look toward a hemispheric lesion (away from the hemiparesis) and can be overcome by reflex maneuvers; pontine gaze palsy cannot.

new_questions.source_quote: the eyes “look toward the lesion” (away from the hemiparetic side) but can be brought to the other side

new_questions.vignette: A 26-year-old woman is brought in unresponsive. She holds her eyelids forcibly shut and resists opening. Her pupils are normal in size and react to light, muscle tone and reflexes are normal, and the doll's eye maneuver produces random movements. Cold caloric testing is performed.
new_questions.question: Which finding on caloric testing would favor psychogenic unresponsiveness over true coma?
options: Classic vestibular nystagmus with a quick component
Tonic deviation of the eyes toward the irrigated ear without nystagmus
No eye movement after 1 minute of observation
Disconjugate deviation with failure of adduction

explanation.why_correct: In psychogenic unresponsiveness caloric testing gives rise to classic vestibular nystagmus, whose quick component requires frontal eye field activity. This quick component is absent in truly comatose patients, who show tonic deviation toward the cold ear.
distractors: Tonic deviation without nystagmus is the response seen in a comatose patient with an intact brainstem.
Absent eye movements after 1 minute of ice water irrigation is the finding expected with loss of brainstem function (as in diagnosis of death by neurologic criteria).
Failure of adduction suggests an MLF lesion in the upper pons, a structural brainstem finding.
explanation.key_point: Nystagmus with a fast phase on caloric testing excludes coma and supports psychogenic unresponsiveness.

new_questions.source_quote: Caloric testing is more helpful because it gives rise to classic vestibular nystagmus with a quick component that requires activity of the frontal eye fields

new_questions.vignette: A comatose 52-year-old man has isolated failure of adduction of the right eye on oculocephalic and caloric testing. Pupils are normal and vertical eye movements are intact.
new_questions.question: Which lesion best explains this finding?
options: Right medial longitudinal fasciculus in the upper pons
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the upper pons
Right oculomotor nerve in the subarachnoid space
Right pontine tegmentum producing horizontal gaze palsy

explanation.why_correct: Isolated failure of ocular adduction with normal pupils and vertical eye movements indicates a lesion of the MLF in the upper pons ipsilateral to the eye that fails to adduct.
distractors: The MLF lesion is ipsilateral to the eye that fails to adduct, so a left-sided lesion is wrong.
An oculomotor nerve lesion would also affect the pupil and vertical eye movements.
A pontine tegmental lesion causing horizontal gaze palsy impairs both eyes' horizontal movements and cannot be overcome by caloric testing.
explanation.key_point: Isolated adduction failure in coma localizes to the ipsilateral MLF in the upper pons.

new_questions.source_quote: indicates a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the upper pons ipsilateral to the eye that fails to adduct
